t: Kth Ancestor of a Tree Node — Binary Lifting Editorial
o: We must answer many queries of the form: starting at `node`, jump exactly k steps up the parent chain and return the resulting node (or -1 if it doesn't exist). In the example, node 3's 1st ancestor is 1, node 5's 2nd ancestor is 0, and node 6 has no 3rd ancestor since its depth is only 2. With n and query count up to 5·10^4, a naive per-query walk is O(n) per query (2.5·10^9 worst case) — too slow. We need preprocessing that lets each query be answered in O(log n), which points to binary lifting: precompute for each node its 2^j-th ancestor.
k: Any k can be decomposed into powers of two, so jumping k steps up = composing jumps of sizes 2^j for each set bit of k.
Precompute up[node][j] = 2^j-th ancestor in O(n log n); each query then costs O(log n).
Store up[node][j] = -1 when the ancestor doesn't exist, so queries naturally return -1.

a.i: For each query, simply follow the parent pointer k times. If we hit the root's -1 before consuming all k steps, return -1. This is trivially correct but each query costs O(depth), up to O(n), which times 5·10^4 queries is too slow for the largest inputs — included mainly as a baseline.
s: Repeat k times: set node = parent[node].
If node becomes -1 at any point, return -1 immediately.
After k successful steps, return node.
a.t: O(n) per query — walking up to n parent links; total O(q·n) worst case.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the stored parent array.

a.i: Build a table up[node][j] = the 2^j-th ancestor of node, using the recurrence up[node][j] = up[up[node][j-1]][j-1] — two half-jumps compose into one full jump. Since k < n ≤ 5·10^4, log2(k) ≤ 16 levels suffice. To answer a query, scan bits of k from high to low; whenever bit j is set, jump via up[node][j]. If any needed ancestor is -1, the answer is -1. Preprocessing is O(n log n) time/space (~800K ints here), and each query is O(log n).
s: Set LOG = ceil(log2(n)) + 1; create table up[n][LOG], with up[v][0] = parent[v].
Fill levels bottom-up: up[v][j] = up[up[v][j-1]][j-1], treating -1 as absorbing (-1 stays -1).
For a query (node, k): iterate j from LOG-1 down to 0.
If bit j of k is set, set node = up[node][j]; if it becomes -1, return -1.
Return node after processing all bits.
a.t: O(n log n) preprocessing to fill the lifting table; O(log n) per query by iterating over the bits of k.
a.sp: O(n log n) for the binary lifting table (~5·10^4 × 17 integers).

w: In an interview, mention brute force briefly, then implement binary lifting — it is the standard technique and generalizes directly to LCA queries. Pitfalls: forgetting that -1 must propagate through the recurrence (guard every lookup), choosing too few levels (use ceil(log2 n)+1), and off-by-one on k vs depth. Edge cases: k equal to or exceeding the node's depth must return -1; node 0 with any k returns -1. Follow-ups often ask for LCA(u, v) via lifting, or handling dynamic trees (link-cut / Euler tour techniques).
